newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bond shortage imminent, brokerage says.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bond shortage imminent, brokerage says.

text.p: Dramatic improvements in Canada's fiscal balance sheet will translate into a shortage of Canadian bonds and a sustained long-term bullish trend in fixed-income markets, said a report released on Friday by one of Canada's largest investment dealers.
The Nesbitt Burns Inc report said the Canadian government had stopped new borrowing for the first time since 1974 and would issue no new bonds a year earlier than expected.
The report, based on a review of weekly data from the Bank of Canada, indicated Canada had been running a financial requirements surplus since May.
Nesbitt Burns called the impending shift in supply of new bonds a "watershed event" that would have a significant impact on Canada's financial landscape.
"You're going to see new issuance of Canadian bonds basically dry up over the course of the next year," said Doug Porter, senior economist with Nesbitt Burns.
"They're shutting off the taps on supply suddenly, yet the demand for fixed-income products is not going to change radically. The adjusting factor will be lower interest rates," Porter said.
A lower federal deficit, which Nesbitt predicted would be about C$5 billion for fiscal 1997/98, was the main catalyst for the shifting supply in fixed-income markets.
Since 1993, Canada has embarked on a sustained budget-cutting project including sharp cuts to program spending, reductions in transfer payments to the 10 provinces and across-the-board tax increases.
Canada's Finance Minister Paul Martin had forecast a C$17 billion deficit for the current fiscal year, but most economists said Martin was at least C$10 billion ahead of his target.
The prospect of government surpluses as early as next year and stable long-term interest rates is good news for Canada's bond market.
"It should make the kinds of gains we've seen in bonds the last couple of years a permanent feature," Porter said.
Porter added that the gaps in supply of new government issues would be absorbed by a higher degree of corporate debt issues in the future.
Canada's benchmark 30-year long bond rose C$0.34 to C$118.63 to yield 6.568 percent in trading on Friday.
The U.S. 30-year bond gained 13/32 to yield 6.53 percent.
The spread between the two benchmark bonds moved to a spread of four basis points.
